John Murray, Ian Dennis & Ali Bruce-Ball have their weekly commentator catch-up. Ali gets richly rewarded at Bournemouth, Ian gets recognised as a famous footballer and John goes walkabout in Nottingham. Hear from Anthony Gordon ahead of England vs Spain in the UEFA Nations League. And who will surge ahead in Clash of the Commentators? articles.title: Euro Leagues - Can Klopp unlock Wirtz? Salah's Trabzon triple & José wants justice! - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Can Klopp unlock Wirtz for Germany? & Jose wants justice after Real's Madrid Derby defeat
articles.body:
Radio 5 Live , · 24 Sep 2026 , · 54 mins

John Bennett is joined by Julien Laurens & Archie Rhind-Tutt on this week's Euro Leagues! The team discuss Liam Rosenior's "don't make a scene" comment after beating Strasbourg, Jose's antics after the Madrid derby, and can 'The New One', Jurgen Klopp, get a tune out of Florian Wirtz as Germany manager in his 44-man squad? We discuss Mo Salah's hattrick for Trabzonspor, and how Freiburg have started the Bundesliga season unbeaten. Then, we hear from PSG's Ballon d'Or contender Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in a sit-down interview with Jules. Why do the guys make him their favourite to win it, and what do they make of Michael Olise's 'moody' post-match interviews? articles.title: Are main stadiums the right place for women's football?
articles.summary: Are main stadiums the right place for womens football?
articles.body:
Where WSL teams play their football continues to be a hot topic and every club approaches things differently.

This usually includes a groundsharing element - either with their men's team, with an EFL team or another sport entirely. For many, this includes both.

But each season, we see incremental shifts in where women's teams play. Over the last six months, Sky Sports have been looking at what the future could hold, including:

How each WSL team groundshares and Chelsea's move at Stamford Bridge

The unique challenge of switching between smaller grounds and main stadiums

How women's football fans and men's football fans are different and those considerations in current stadiums, including Goodison Park and the Joie Stadium

New WSL Football guidelines and how they might be implemented

How WSL fans are outspending Premier League fans at matches and the WSL's alcohol trial

Are purpose-built stadiums the future? Plus a case study of KC Current

Manchester United and Liverpool groundshare with rugby teams, while Tottenham, West Ham, Brighton and London City Lionesses all play at lower league club grounds.

Everton and Man City also have their own designated stadiums that they do not share with another senior team.

Most of these also play a handful of games at the club’s main ground. These are usually marquee matches against those in the top four or local rivals to entice fans, with more space for both serious and casual supporters to attend.

For example, Liverpool often play the Merseyside derby at Anfield and attract a big crowd, while Manchester City and Chelsea hosted each other at the Etihad and Stamford Bridge respectively last season.

London City do not have a men's club ground to fall back on, but have to have another option in case the Copperjax Community Stadium is unavailable.

This happened in March. Due to fixtures being changed, they played their home WSL fixture against Chelsea at The Den, rather than at Bromley.

This was not well received by some Millwall Lionesses fans - the club's women's team - due to the history between the two. They accused London City of "stealing" Millwall's position in the women's game, leading the EFL club to apologise.

They added they had no further plans to host London City beyond the Chelsea fixture, and would reinvest any revenue into Millwall Lionesses.

Across London, West Ham have not played a game at the London Stadium since 2019, which has been a contentious point among some players in recent years.

However, they face a unique challenge in that the club do not own the stadium and the current concession agreement in place only covers men's matches, friendlies and some youth games.

Should the women's team play there, there would need to be a large hosting charge - which is significantly higher than the men’s matches - something that the women’s budget would not be able to accommodate.

That being said, the Hammers have enjoyed a record-breaking season at the Chigwell Construction Stadium in recent history, adding to the notion that smaller grounds, played at consistently, can be vital.

Some teams are more active at their club's main grounds.

Arsenal play all of their WSL games at the Emirates Stadium, along with Champions League knockout fixtures, but still play cup games and Champions League league phase matches at Meadow Park - another two-way share.

But the Gunners have honed in on their unique fan culture, setting up the 'Block by Block' initiative, consulting supporters on how the Emirates can look and feel like home for the women's team.

Different fans have been invited to attend sessions, contributing to murals, flags and music. Arsenal players have also been included.

And by far and away, they have the highest attendance in the WSL with an average of over 33,000.

But playing at the Emirates does come with logistical challenges, especially when the men’s team are also used to going deep in competitions - both teams have reached the semi-finals of the Champions League last season.

From the football calendar to staffing to grounds work, to have the women's team also play full-time at the Emirates would be a precarious balancing act, and is likely a key factor behind the continued use of Borehamwood.

However, three WSL teams are already full-time residents at their club's main ground. Two are newly promoted this season - Charlton at The Valley and Birmingham at St Andrew's - with Aston Villa playing all of their games at Villa Park.

Aston Villa head coach Natalia Arroyo told Sky Sports : "It's a privilege and it's still special, even if it's our every day when we play home.

"We need to do our best to excite the fans to come to us. Today it was 3,000, let's see if tomorrow it can be 3,001 and tomorrow 4,000 so that we can really create this atmosphere at Villa Park.

"If we are winning, scoring goals and playing exciting football, people will come.

"I know the club is investing in having different things to do around the game to bring people back, so what we feel we can do, we are trying to do."

Sharing the same ground does present a ‘one club’ mentality, that the women's teams are integrated into the fabric of a club and are important to its future.

Interestingly, over 50 per cent of WSL2 teams also play at their club’s main stadium.

Some might suggest that having a permanent home at the club’s main ground is the ultimate goal. It offers space for far more fans than smaller grounds, and with the right marketing and matches, can attract impressive crowds - Arsenal have proven that can happen on a regular basis.

They had played all of their Champions League matches at the ground last term, but have now moved away from their Kingsmeadow home.

The ground in Kingston, south West London, was the first stadium owned solely by a women's club, and they had played there for almost a decade.

Since Chelsea moved to Kingsmeadow (2017/18) in the WSL: P80, W69 D6, L5 with an 86.3 per cent win percentage and average 2.7 points per game Chelsea at Stamford Bridge in the WSL: P15, W13, D1, L1 with an 86.7 per cent win percentage and average of 2.7 points per game.

Up until November 2020, Chelsea had shared with AFC Wimbledon, before the League One club moved to Plough Lane. The Blues will now play their Champions League league phase and home domestic cup games from this season at the Dons' ground, with Kingsmeadow - which had been exclusively used for the women's team - used in other capacities.

Discussing the move to Stamford Bridge, Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor exclusively told Sky Sports: "The women's game is growing and we need to make sure we follow and we also initiate that group. We want to be really ambitious, really top in terms of what we do off and on the pitch. That's the right time for us to do that.

"Even if we already as a club achieve a lot, we still have room for improvement and being able to offer the best experience for the fans, but also for the players. They want to play in the biggest stadiums. The Bridge is a really historic stadium where we created already a lot of memories."

While it is a bold statement of intent, there are certainly parallels with Arsenal, as the Blues look to cultivate the same atmosphere their rivals have done in their successful move to the Emirates.

As has been established though, a key argument for WSL teams remaining at smaller grounds is making them sell-outs and generating noisy home support.

That is something Chelsea have had at Kingsmeadow, which has given them a massive advantage. How that will translate to Stamford Bridge remains to be seen. A lot of work has to be done to make it a success.

Something that Chelsea might look to do is not opening the whole ground, but this also comes with pitfalls.

Only parts of Villa Park are used for their WSL teams and the atmosphere generated is not as intense as other stadiums.

For Man City's Head of Women's and Girls Football, Hannah Dingley , it is why her team are not considering a move away from the Joie Stadium any time soon.

“We've seen this with other teams that if we were in a position to sell out the Etihad, we'd be playing at the Etihad,” she told Sky Sports.

“You don't make the best atmosphere if you play in a half empty stadium, so playing in the Joie is perfect. It's full, it's lively, it's bouncing and it's home.

“But equally we need to grow and if you want to do that, then you need to push yourself to try and sell out the Etihad. That's what we've tried to do this year and that will grow over time as that fan base grows.

“But it's chicken and egg - we need to grow that fan base so that then we can go on and fill that stadium.”

And it shows in their average points-per-game at home this season too - the highest in the league, and was huge factor behind their first WSL title win in ten years.

But for their part, Aston Villa - and Leicester last season - ranked among the lowest in the league for average points-per-game at home, which was also reflected in their league position.

Discussing Leicester specifically, Sky Sports WSL commentator Ellen Ellard added: "It can't be an easy situation to play in. It feels really distant from the fans, even when you do get crowds of over a thousand. It really doesn't feel like it in there with how big the stadium is and how spread out the fans are.

"The previous Leicester manager, Amandine Miquel, did speak about the benefit of the pitch. It was so well maintained that they did not have many injuries and it was important for keeping up the standard of football.

"You have a home advantage in some ways if your pitch is of higher quality, but you don't have it in terms of fans being able to generate a noise.

"With the smaller stadiums or the women's specific stadiums, they really keep in the noise."

The unique challenge of switching between stadiums

Women's teams often switch between two grounds for their home matches, needing to get used to different pitches and surroundings quickly.

It somewhat dilutes the concept of home advantage. A team could go weeks without playing at their regular home ground if they have a run of away games, fixtures played at their club’s main ground or an international break.

But larger capacities turn more eyes onto the women’s football. Growth is still a key aim for the game and if you can entice fans to come to one match, they will hopefully continue to support the team in others.

It also gives the women’s game the weight of a name behind it, a commitment to its future and a glimpse of what that could be.

Then, there are the considerations for the teams themselves.

Discussing the differences at Meadow Park, Arsenal head coach Renee Slegers explained : “The changing room is smaller so we have to think more about how many people do we have in there, how are we effective with space and a little bit with set-up issues.

“Then the benches are closer to each other so you're much closer to the opposition. You can almost see and feel each other, so you have to be very aware of your communication.

“But I love to play at both stadiums because Meadow Park is also a historical ground for Arsenal Women and it's a very intimate setting."

Communication is key in any football game between the bench and players. Most WSL teams are used to this being relatively easy, with smaller crowds making less noise.

But dugouts can be further away at larger stadiums and the pitches can be bigger, making communication more of a challenge.

When asked about that prospect when playing Arsenal at the Emirates, Spurs boss Martin Ho said in March: "It’s making sure the players stick together, communicate with one another and use moments to lift each other through the game.

"They’re not going to hear everything from us as staff, so it's giving them a lot of clarity and understanding of what we want to do and how we want to approach the game.

"Everyone should have some leadership moments where they support one another, and leaning on one another when you're playing in these stadiums.

"We've maybe not had a lot of these moments where it's packed every single week. We had one at Manchester City, which was quite noisy. We've had some at home at Brisbane Road where it's full, we've had some at the [Tottenham Hotspur] stadium.

"But we know the Emirates brings more noise, more expectation, more pressure, but you play as a professional to embrace that and enjoy it."

"There are many benefits, but we have to be really balanced. It's hard to sell them out - these are the biggest stadiums in England, and the men's game has had time to develop and grow."

EFL grounds are more suspectable to the elements as well. In February, Brighton postponed their match against Arsenal at the Broadfield Stadium an hour and a half before kick-off due to a waterlogged pitch.

And for Hannah Buckley - Head of Safety, Sustainability and Infrastructure for WSL Football - one of the benefits of playing at a club's main ground is better infrastructure which is able to handle unpredictable weather and avoiding a build-up of fixtures.

She explained: "From a player's point of view, the quality of the playing surface guarantees the fixtures will be scheduled.

"Player arrival, safety and security is also a big piece of the jigsaw. Very often the buses go in underneath the stadiums, and then the players have a route to the dressing room.

"In terms of scale, even thinking about the size of the changing rooms, the size of the squads, and then things like dressing rooms for the MDT (multi-disciplinary team) and the coaches or media obligations.

"From a fan point of view, there's more seats and the food, beverages and hospitality on offer is broader and wider.

"But from my point of view, it's thinking about all the different users on a match day, whether you are the grounds person, for example, you might have undersoil heating.

"Or if you are the written journalist, the content creator, or even the analyst, the technology that's available to you in the stadium to be able to deliver high quality outputs.

Sky Sports' Harriet Prior also sees why the switching works for many WSL teams, saying: "I prefer attending WSL games at their individual stadiums because it brings its own vibe.

"The stadiums are fuller and generally has a better atmosphere and feels more personalised to the women’s team, rather than at the larger men’s stadium, which can sometimes be a bit emptier with not as many fans.

"But I really like that exhibition matches are played at bigger stadiums, for example when Liverpool play Everton at Anfield. They always attract a big crowd and it feels like a big game.

"It’s a good touch point to get fans who don’t generally engage with the women’s team into the game. That’s a major plus point to integrate fans.

"When you have a team like Arsenal who are packing out the Emirates week in, week out, that’s where you can see the benefits of it because the atmosphere is electric and it feels like you’re at a huge game every single week."

Women’s football fans are different from men’s fans

While the game of football may be similar on the pitch, off it the fans of women’s and men’s football wildly differ.

Women’s football is a far more inclusive, safe space for female fans, the LGBTQ+ community and families and stadiums need to cater for a vastly different fanbase.

For most grounds, that is a hard balance to strike with many set up for men’s football and their fans, largely male.

These considerations are what led WSL Football to publish new guidelines aimed to help build or upgrade venues for women’s teams.

The range of topics were substantial, from female-friendly changing rooms and toilet facilities, parent/guardian orientated spaces, plus considerations around safety for a primarily female fanbase.

Buckley led the way on producing the guidelines and gave an insight on how she foresees them being implemented

"We have a stadium strategy for all of our clubs and one of the objectives of that was about recognising there was a gap in the marketplace," she said.

"There was no guidance around what the female fan or player needed and when we pulled a working group together with industry specialists and clubs, there was a clear recognition of needing to look at what's different.

"We can't always move walls in current stadiums, or put more seats in because it might reduce capacity, because it wasn't designed for those purposes so the guidance document is for everyone - those starting afresh and those with current infrastructure.

" There are a number of our clubs who are looking at their long-term venue strategy. With the growth of the game, the calendar congestion, we've got to be very mindful of trying to get primacy in stadiums so we can schedule at the times that we need to and to service our fans and broadcasters.

"This is version one, and there'll be version two, three, four, five, as clubs build and we learn, because the important thing to remember is we're at the start of our journey around stadium development.

"We've got to make sure we're agile and are fit for purpose for the future of the game and all of the users to make sure the business plan can stack financially."

"The owners were very keen for it to feel like Everton Women's stadium. They did not want us to feel like it was the men's stadium and we now just play there."

Last season, Everton moved their women's team from Walton Hall Park to Goodison Park after the men's team vacated their famous home for the newly-built Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The club has had to adapt an existing men's ground for its female team and their fans, with Director of Women’s Football Operations, Catherine Wright , said: "It’s a longer-term project, but we identified some critical areas that we thought would be the most impactful for the first season. We really prioritised the player spaces and the branding around the stadiums.

"In terms of branding, instantly when people walk in, it will look and felt different to what it had been before. We rebranded within the colour palette of the club using blue and pink with more prominence of the pink than you have with the men's branding.

"We also have ‘seat curls’ that cover some of the empty seats because we had to recognise where we were with attendances. We didn't want it to feel like we were playing in an empty stadium - that was important to the players.

"So the the lower tiers on three side are open and then the tiers above that and on the fourth side have been covered in branded seat curls.

"We also spoke with our players and asked what was important to them in the tunnel areas and the player spaces.

"One of the big things was having a space for their family and friends so we identified a lounge within Goodison and we changed that to be called 'the Mo Marley Lounge', so our player families have somewhere to go before the match and somewhere to wait after.

"In the tunnel areas and dressing room, we had some simple, quick wins - removing urinals for instance. We also got all new showers to make them a bit nicer.

"We put in additional storage so every seat unit has a name placard for each player so it feels more personal.

"We put in cupboards so they have places to store jewellery and phones and we moved hooks down because women are shorter than men generally.

"One of the key things for them too was mirrors because when they leave that dressing room, they're on a world stage and it's important for them to look their best.

"We also put baby changes in there so if there's any players with babies that might need to be in the tunnel area, for example if a player is still breastfeeding, a partner or whoever might bring the child and wait in that area for them.

"We had put in a new anti-doping section. In the men's game, we rarely used the two referee changing rooms so often, the second referee changing room was used for anti-doping.

"We didn't have that option because virtually every week, we've got mixed referees so both of those rooms are in use.

"Then the next phase will be more around fan areas and fan seating.

"Our attendances are growing, but they're still quite modest so we've got time to look at the wider changes around the stadium that will support that growth.

"We have done a lot of things already like our fan zone, for instance. We recognised that our fans are very different to the make-up of men's fans, so we've moved our fan zones into the concourses because they're bigger spaces where people can keep dry.

"That's quite important when you've got young children because you don't want them getting wet and then sat outside for an hour and a half.

"But increasing the numbers of baby changes and female toilet ratios are among the area we need to address."

On the pitch, Everton did not win at their new ground until February, beating Aston Villa 2-1, but did win their first home game at Goodison in the 2026/27 campaign against Charlton. Overall, they have warned 12 WSL points at the ground since the start of last season.

Everton have also had a change in manager - Scott Phelan replacing Brian Sorensen on an interim basis in February - which ironically came after that first home victory - before taking the role full time.

Reflecting on that, Toffees goalkeeper Courtney Brosnan said: "We were desperate to get our first win at Goodison because we know how amazing it is to be able to play at the stadium, but I don't think it's anything to do with being at Goodison. There’s other factors.

"We're coming into each game wanting to win and that took a little bit longer than we had anticipated or wanted. We want to make it our home and a fortress so it's nice to now have those wins under the belt and continue to look forward."

Brosnan also reflected on the changes made at Goodison Park to make it feel like home for the women's team.

She added: "At Walton Hall Park, the pitch was great but we didn't have as much room, so it's been amazing in terms of the space for our pre-match, in the changing room and the medical and physio facilities as well.

"That's been a big difference and makes the preparations for the game a lot easier.

"They were good with us in terms of asking us specifics of what we wanted in the changing room, even if it's something small like mirrors, it's just making us the most comfortable and confident going into the games.

"We played a lot of the derbies at Goodison Park [before moving there] and few games throughout the season. It did already feel like home and you're used to the pitch and the things it has to offer. It definitely made the transition easier.

"It's also really cool when you're walking out and you can see all the banners [from the fans] because there's a lot more space. In terms of atmosphere, having fans behind both goals and on that one side as well, it's really exciting."

The experience as a whole is different and we need facilities that are supportive of that for the game to grow and for us to be able to sell out those bigger stadiums.

One ground that has catered for a female fanbase for some time is the Joie Stadium. Dingley explained how catering to the right demographic can help retention – which in turn, would expand growth and the potential move into larger capacity stadiums.

She said: “We've all experienced it as women - I've been to many a men's game and I never have to queue for the toilet, then you go to a women's game and you miss half of the second half because of the queue.

“There's definitely differences in the make-up of the fan base that we need to consider.

“One of the things we're really proud of at the Joie is having a buggy park, and when you need more spaces for kids to be able to run around and have their face painted or things like that, fans that come to the women's game don't want to crowd on a terrace. We want to be a bit more comfortable.

“The experience as a whole is different and we need facilities that are supportive of that for the game to grow and for us to be able to sell out those bigger stadiums.

“We need to make sure that the experience of the fans that are coming now is top so that they don't just use it as a one-off, that they want to come every week and they really engage in the sport.”

The Joie is perhaps an easier example with the ground used primarily for the women's senior team, but this is not so easy elsewhere.

Asked how current grounds are taking female teams and fans into consideration, Buckley added: "We are seeing clubs find ways to deliver solutions.

"It might not always look how you think it might, but the fact they've never had to think about some things until now is a great example of clubs having to think outside the box in terms of finding solutions.

"Sometimes they're operational solutions as opposed to physical infrastructure solutions, but it's about recognising that with all of our clubs where they need to invest.

"For example, we've got players returning from maternity leave and clubs are having to think about how they can facilitate, for example, breastfeeding rooms.

"It's also important thing to stress we only launched in November. Most works take place in the off season, so hopefully all of our clubs are making good use of the document."

Research shows WSL fans spending more to attend games

In an additional and somewhat surprising difference, data from Barclays earlier this year revealed that WSL fans, on average, spend more when they attend games than Premier League fans.

The research - which excludes ticket prices - looked at spending across the 2024/25 season, and how football fans spend inside stadiums and in the local economy, such as in pubs, restaurants, shops and local transport.

Premier League fans who attended at least one match in person during the 2024/25 season say they attended seven games on average, supporting local economies by choosing to spend £138 throughout the day.

During the same season, WSL fans who saw at least one match opted to attend four times on average, spending £144.70.

Based on average matchday attendances, this equates to combined discretionary fan spending of £5.6m per Premier League matchday, and just under £1m (£988k) per WSL matchday, totalling £2.3bn across both seasons.

Across both the Premier League and WSL, spending within a 1km radius of stadiums rises by an average of 4.1 per cent on matchdays.

Regionally, the north of England performs particularly strongly, with local spending rising by 5.2 per cent, compared with 3.5 per cent in the south.

At the same time, London-based clubs see an average local spending uplift of 5.6 per cent on matchdays, while clubs outside the capital see a 2.8 per cent increase.

One initiative that might have had an impact is a trial that allowed supporters to drink alcohol in the stands.

Legislation introduced in 1985 to combat hooliganism made it illegal for fans to drink alcohol in view of the pitch in the top five tiers of men's football in England and Wales.

However, women's football has never been included in the ban and in the 2024/25 season, four WSL2 clubs took part in the initial phase of the trial.

This was then expanded for the 2025/26 campaign, where seven WSL teams - including Chelsea, Arsenal, Man City and Man Utd - joined, alongside a further three WSL2 clubs.

Overall, 15 of the 26 WSL Football clubs took part - with shareholders approving the overall introduction of alcohol in the stands over the summer after a successful 18-month trial in which the consumption of alcohol was found to have not had a detrimental impact on the welcoming environment at women's matches.

A survey of the trial by WSL Football involving 4,270 fans found the average rating for fan safety was 9.4 out of 10, while 70 per cent were in favour of alcohol at games.

There was also an average score of 9.1 when asked about the family-friendly environment at games, with match officials also not reporting a change in fan behaviour.

Are purpose-built stadiums the next step?

There could be another UK women’s football first on the horizon and one that might pave the way for more radical change.

It will be built on land called Bennett's Field, which is adjacent to the Amex Stadium near the ground's East Stand. It will be linked with the current main ground via a bridge link and will have a minimum capacity of 10,000.

The Seagulls had initially wanted the ground to be ready for the start of the 2027/28 campaign, but is is now hoped the stadium will be open no later than the start of the 2030/31 season.

Brighton chief executive and deputy chairman Paul Barber was quizzed on the size of the ground, and whether it will still be viable in a few years time as the women's team continues to grow.

He replied: "Right sizing is really important for women’s football as well as being ambitious, but not overly ambitious.

"Putting on top-class football matches in stadiums that are too big can be detrimental because it can give a sense to the crowd that not everyone cares as much as they do, not everybody wants to be there and therefore it’s not such a big event.

"If you’ve got a right-sized stadium and it’s full and noisy and everyone feels like ‘this is something I want to be at’ – which women’s football is and should be and will be even bigger in the future.

"We feel for a club our size, it’s about the right size for some time to come.

"If it explodes, if we get to that lovely position where we’re regularly sold out and people are clamouring for tickets, we do have a neighbouring stadium where we might be able to switch our biggest games.

"But that’s way into the future. We’re regularly getting two or three thousand people to watch our women’s team at the moment and if we can triple that, that would be amazing.

"We’re right-sizing for our city, for our club and what we see as the growth of women’s football in the next period."

The stadium will incudes bespoke changing and recovery rooms and pitches for female athletes all the way through to catering for a more inclusive fan base.

"We're demanding from the women's team the same level of high performance as we are from the men's team," Barber added.

"For me, it's logical to provide the best possible facilities to get that performance. We've done it at the training ground so we should do it with the stadium as well.

"The economics are so weighted towards the men's game at the moment, if there's a clash over dates for fixtures, the men's team takes priority because that's where the significant income comes in.

"If you've got a purpose-built stadium for women's football, that goes away. The women's team will play in that stadium when they need to play in it and it will be suitable for them."

And Brighton are not the only team in the UK to be planning for a more bespoke future for their women's team.

WSL2 side Durham announced in March 2025 that they were teaming up with the Durham Women's cricket team to build a state-of-the-art facility dedicated to women's sport in Chester-le-Street.

This would include a football high performance centre, new training facilities and crucially, a new stadium, creating the Riverside sporting complex.

They currently play at Durham University's sports ground at Maiden Castle, while the cricket team share the Seat Unique Riverside with the men's side.

There are few purpose-built stadiums in the world for women’s teams, let alone the UK.

One of those though is in Kansas City, Missouri, where National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) side KC Current play, co-owned by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and his wife Brittany Mahomes - a former footballer herself - as well as businesspeople Chris and Angie Long.

It has proven to be a wild success. In the last two years, KC Current have sold out every home game with the team and the ground - called the CPKC Stadium - becoming a beloved community entity.

"We looked at the financial model around sports broadly, and in this case, being an owner of a women's professional football team," Chris Long exclusively told Sky Sports. " One thing we noticed really quickly was no great franchise doesn’t have its own facilities.

"We wanted this sense of ownership and we thought that it would elevate everything - elevate the play, the culture and the feeling for the city – and it has.

"It brought that feeling of ownership to the broader region and people are really proud that it's our own.

"It's a community asset and everybody gets to participate in attending games, attending and hosting events and being part of something that'll be generational."

KC Current's record at the CPKC Stadium in all competitions: W38 D2 L9.

This season, KC Current have a home record of W8 D4 L0 at home and W3 D1 L9 away.

But as is the case for many trailblazers, it was not an easy process to get off the ground, especially in terms of funding. The ownership group visited 40 banks - only one saw women's football as a viable investment and said yes.

"When we decided to do this, not a lot of people were positive on it," Long said. "They said ‘go and play in the men's stadium, you're wasting money, use the location for something else’.

"However, we felt like if you put something forth and be the precedent, it's really going to capture the world's attention, because it's something that's meaningful.

"But nobody wanted to finance it. There was no benchmark for what a women's stadium looked like.

"We would say ‘we're going to sell the naming rights’, and they would discount it by 50 per cent. Or ‘here's what we think attendance will be’, and we'd get that discounted, and on and on to the point where there wasn't support to finance it based on those types of projections.

"Also, at that point, valuations for women's teams were really low, certainly in the gap between men's and women's, so you couldn't even use the men's side as a precedent.

"We didn't have public funding, it was all done privately, so the financing was a huge piece of the of the puzzle.

"Having your own stadium opens up so many revenue levers that, in the case of women's sports, haven't been properly utilised, like naming rights, gates, the way you do your premium, you design it all, the way you do all the branding around the stadium - everything is yours.

"We felt really convicted that that was a massive swing in revenue that would help us."

Once the finances were secured, the stadium took just 18 months to build and opened in March 2024. It was a process that needed to be quickened as their lease at their former ground, Sporting Park - where MLS side Sporting KC play - was due to expire.

Having their own stadium has given Current a significant competitive advantage too.

Long explained: "It’s so loud. There’s a sea of teal and when the team goes into their locker room, it's not a second locker room at someone else's stadium, even for a home game. It's theirs.

"Opposing players and coaches haven't been shy about saying it's a super intimidating place to play. For all the reasons our team likes it are the reasons other teams find it a daunting task.

"When you can get any advantage in sports - and you do it in a legal manner like infrastructure - you take it because live sports is one of the hardest things to get an edge in."

With KC Current paving the way, other teams in the NWSL especially are now following their lead, with Denver Summit set to open their own purpose-built stadium in 2028.

"I knew we wouldn't be the last," Long said. "Denver are putting a massive amount of investment into infrastructure with their new team.

"Boston are renovating an existing stadium in a great location outside of the Boston area and we are constantly fielding calls across the world of others that want to do it.

"I feel like there's been the new wave of thinking that has existed in men's sports forever. In the MLS alone, their first stadiums were built over 25 years ago.

"But this is the moment for women's sports and infrastructure and I can't wait to see what we look like, not even in 10 years, but in five years when a lot of these projects really catch their momentum."

Interviews conducted by Charlotte Marsh, Hayley Fox and Sky Sports News, with thanks to....

Hannah Dingley and Man City; Chris Long, KC Current and Dan Johnson; Hannah Buckley and WSL Football; Renee Slegers and Arsenal; Natalia Arroyo and Aston Villa; Martin Ho and Tottenham; Sonia Bompastor and Chelsea; West Ham and Brighton; Harriet Prior and Ellen Ellard; Catherine Wright, Courtney Brosnan and Everton

articles.title: Torcedora do Santos mobiliza orações em luta contra o câncer | G1
articles.standfirst: A comissária de bordo e influenciadora digital Natalia Potira, de 39 anos, ganhou uma enorme corrente de orações mobilizada pelo Santos Futebol Clube.
articles.summary: A comissária de bordo e influenciadora digital Natalia Potira, de 39 anos, ganhou uma enorme corrente de orações mobilizada pelo Santos Futebol Clube.
articles.body:
A comissária de bordo e influenciadora digital Natalia Potira, de 39 anos, conhecida como Naty Potira ou Potirão, enfrenta uma luta contra o câncer metastático e está internada há cerca de um mês. Fanática pelo Santos Futebol Clube, a torcedora ganhou uma enorme corrente de orações mobilizada pelo time nas redes sociais.

O clube fez uma publicação convocando a nação santista a enviar boas energias para Naty. A torcedora recebeu apoio de diversos artistas e jogadores , inclusive de Neymar Jr.

Naty Potira é torcedora fanática do Santos FC — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Em maio, Neymar chegou a dar uma camisa para a influenciadora pessoalmente e, no mês passado , ele dedicou a vitória contra o Corinthians para ela. O vídeo da homenagem foi enviado para Naty quando ela já estava internada, no dia 30 de agosto (assista acima) .

"Vocês sabem o tamanho do amor que eu tenho por esse time! Estar longe por motivo do meu tratamento me deixa com o coração apertadinho… Mas nada que uma vitória num clássico, e receber esse carinho especial do meu ídolo, não resolva né?", escreveu a influenciadora, após ver o vídeo.

Naty Potira já ganhou abraço, camisa e homenagem de Neymar, além de fazer publicidade com o jogador — Foto: Reprodução

Segundo apurado pelo g1 , Naty luta contra o câncer há três anos, mas nunca quis tornar colocar a doença como pauta de sua vida. Em 2023, ela chegou a compartilhar nas redes sociais o diagnóstico de câncer de colo de útero e, no ano seguinte, revelou que havia se curado.

Apesar disso, a influenciadora retomou o tratamento contra a doença cerca de um mês depois, devido ao quadro de metástase (processo pelo qual células cancerígenas se desprendem do tumor primário, circulam pela corrente sanguínea e se instalam em outras partes do corpo).

Ao g1 , o namorado dela Guilherme Kastner explicou que Naty não deixou o tratamento interferir na rotina e seguiu se cuidando, com alto astral e muita esperança, evitando falar sobre o prognóstico da doença. Ela chegou a se livrar de tumores no pescoço e no colo do útero por duas vezes , mas, recentemente, passou a sofrer com a doença na área abdominal.

A influenciadora está internada há 29 dias e, desde domingo (21), está sedada, em um hospital na capital paulista. A torcedora do Santos recebe o carinho de amigos, familiares, artistas e fãs por meio do namorado, que está de acompanhante e repassa todas as mensagens para Naty.

Naty Potira começou a torcer para o Santos FC por influência do pai — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Conhecida nas redes sociais pelo conteúdo sobre o Santos FC, Naty se tornou torcedora do time alvinegro por influência do pai, que morreu em 2024 em decorrência de um câncer.

Ela é comissária de bordo e apresentadora do programa de uma rádio na capital paulista, mas também já participou de outro podcast sobre futebol, vídeos na Cazé TV e já fez publicidade para uma marca junto com Neymar.

Naty Potira é comissária de bordo e foi apresentadora de podcast do Santos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Naty namora o head de conteúdo do Santos FC, Guilherme Kastner, há quase três anos. Eles estiveram juntos na Copa do Mundo de 2026, nos Estados Unidos.

De acordo com Guilherme, ela iria para a competição fazer um trabalho, mas teve uma interferência de saúde e precisou ser internada para um procedimento em junho. Apesar disso, Naty se recuperou a tempo de viajar para o jogo do Brasil contra o Haiti em uma surpresa feita pelo namorado.

Naty Potira namora Guilherme Kastner há quase três anos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

articles.title: Ballon d'Or: The case for Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe and the main favourites assessed
articles.summary: Will Harry Kane become the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or since 2001, or will Lamine Yamal become the youngest winner in history? Will Kylian Mbappe be crowned after becoming the all-time World Cup top scorer - or could holder Ousmane Dembele retain his crown?
articles.body:
We've assessed all the runners and riders for the most prestigious personal gong in football...

Harry Kane set the record to become the fastest player to 100 goals in the history of the Bundesliga earlier this month.

He didn't just set it, he smashed it, reaching his ton in 98 games - 31 faster than the previous holder, Dieter Muller, whose record had stood for almost half a century.

That was underpinned by the most prolific scoring season of his entire career in 2025/26, netting 36 goals in 31 Bundesliga matches as well as 14 in 13 Champions League matches and, if that wasn't enough, a further 12 strikes for England including six at the World Cup.

Already the best No 9 in the world, Kane has somehow found a way to hit new heights even in his 30s.

Scoring 73 goals in 65 games is, simply, mindblowing. And a fitting reward for maintaining his fitness better than he ever has before - having arrived at previous international tournaments already clearly burnt out.

Others may have picked up bigger team honours but for an individual award, there has been no player in better form on the planet. And what better time to pick up the award than in his home town when the winner is crowned at the London Palladium next month? Ron Walker

The case for the poster boy of the World Cup champions winning the Ballon d'Or does go a long way to making itself. Not that it's stopped Lamine Yamal from quite publicly adding to it, saying this week the award should go to a "unique" player and was not all about goals.

Whether that was a slight on his main rival Kane or not, Lamine Yamal is in esteemed company in his aims of lifting the greatest personal accolade in world football with five of the last seven winners in World Cup years coming from teams who reached the final.

Though goals might not be top of Lamine Yamal's mind, he will point to his own career-best scoring feats of 25 strikes for club and country across 2025/26, including three in the Champions League knock-out stages. That made him the youngest-ever player to reach the 40-goal tally for Barca, an impressive feat considering the esteemed company he sits among.

Only one of those quarter-century of goals came at the World Cup but his tournament, much like his season, was not lacking in the kind of entertainment, energy and stepovers which he feels, and many will agree, should lead to a Ballon d'Or victory.

He would become the youngest ever winner should he get his hands on the trophy in October but that should count for him, rather than against him, given the feats he has hit while spending every game bar the World Cup semi-final and final as an 18-year-old last season.

If you're good enough, you're old enough - and there's already no question in this case. Ron Walker

Kylian Mbappe: Give the World Cup all-time top goalscorer his dues

This one feels like it has to be inevitable at some point, right?

The fact that Kylian Mbappe has competed in two World Cup finals - one of which he won and the other he scored a hat-trick in - and still has yet to be recognised as the best player in the world, seems incredible.

The heir apparent to Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo is still waiting. Could this be his year?

So far this calendar year, the Frenchman has scored 31 goals, including 10 during a record-breaking World Cup campaign where he became the competition's all-time top scorer.

While Les Bleus' elimination in the semi-final and subsequent defeat to England in the third-place play-off may hurt his chances, he is arguably the most high-profile player to never win it.

Surely his crowning moment has to come sooner rather than later? And perhaps his exploits over the summer will be enough. He certainly seems to think it will.

"I made a lot of history this summer in the biggest competition in the world," he said when probed about his chances.

"I have a feeling it could be a good year for that [to win the Ballon d'Or]." Callum Bishop

Rodri's Ballon d'Or chances looked remote at the end of an injury-hit domestic season in which he only made 22 Premier League and Champions League starts for Manchester City.

But it doesn't get any bigger than the World Cup. Spain's winning captain in the summer, and the recipient of the Golden Ball prize as the best player of the tournament, demands serious consideration.

Winning the World Cup's best player award helped Luka Modric clinch the Ballon d'Or in 2018 and Rodri, while not the favourite, is entitled to feel he has a shot of repeating that feat and winning the coveted prize for a second time after his 2024 success. Nick Wright

Ousmane Dembele: The reigning champion keeping it consistent

Ousmane Dembele entered the year with the difficult task of following up his 2025 Ballon d'Or triumph, but another influential campaign at Paris Saint-Germain has put him firmly in contention to win the prize.

The France forward has scored 20 times for PSG and played a key role as Luis Enrique's side retained the Champions League, including scoring in the final against Arsenal. He carried that form into the World Cup too, registering six goals and two assists as France reached the semi-finals.

Winning successive Ballon d'Or awards is a rare feat, but Dembele has built a compelling case. Another European crown, combined with his most productive major international tournament, means the reigning holder has plenty of reasons to believe he can keep hold of the trophy. Isaac Kinghorn-Eastlake

Bruno Fernandes: The assist record breaker

In the last 20 years, there have been just two Premier League players to win the Ballon d'Or. Rodri was the most recent in 2024. The other was a Portuguese star who was the focal point of everything good about Manchester United's attack.

That was, of course, Cristiano Ronaldo in 2008. However, that same description can be used to describe Bruno Fernandes last season.

Admittedly, the fact that United didn't play in Europe or win a major trophy last season does not help Fernandes' cause. However, it didn't stop him from sweeping up the honours in English football.

If anything, the fact he is part of the current Manchester United side and not the one Ronaldo had the benefit of playing with in 2008 should give him more credit. A record-breaking 21 assists would've been impressive in a title-winning team, let alone one that had finished 15th the year before.

Had he lifted the World Cup, Fernandes' case would've been among the strongest. But, when talking about individual campaigns, very few had the same impact as the 'Portuguese magnifico's'. Callum Bishop

Erling Haaland: The goal machine should be closer to favourites

I will state from the outset that I believe there to be more worthy Ballon d'Or candidates than Erling Haaland for this year's prize. But I also believe he should be higher in the pecking order, closer to the coveted trophy than many assume him to be.

No doubt he will be a recipient of this award in years to come. Probably more than once. At his projected pace, he will beat both Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo to 1,000 career goals.

I also think he deserves more credit for the talismanic figure he has developed into at such a young age, only just turned 26.

He was king of the Vikings for Norway this summer. He's been transformational for the Premier League since he joined in 2022. Revolutionary for Manchester City's cause, too. 169 goals in 205 appearances is a freakishly ridiculous rate at which to score goals.

It may not be now, but you are looking at a Ballon d'Or winner of future generations. Laura Hunter

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia: The Champions League's best player as PSG retain title

Winning the Ballon d'Or in a World Cup year when your country did not make it to the World Cup is virtually impossible but Khvicha Kvaratskhelia has a shot. That is because he was the best player in the Champions League last season and it was not close.

Nobody scored more goals than Kvaratskhelia in the knockout stages of the tournament, while he finished the campaign with the most assists from open play too. The Georgia international has been the catalyst behind Paris Saint-Germain's ascent.

They were a fine team with Bradley Barcola on the left wing. Kvaratskhelia made PSG better, a ceaseless energy that upped their pressing game and added quality too. You can find out more about why he would be a worthy winner of the Ballon d'Or here . Adam Bate

articles.title: Sin salario ni equipo, entrena con plátanos y azucarillos... y pide un deseo: "Si no ayudan, lo pierdo todo"
articles.standfirst: Amaniel Desta, una oportunidad mundialista para no dejar de soñar: cuarto en el Tour de Ruanda y uno de los jóvenes más constantes del calendario africano, buscará en el Mundial de Canadá un escaparate para los equipos europeos de cara a 2027
articles.summary: Amaniel Desta, una oportunidad mundialista para no dejar de soñar: cuarto en el Tour de Ruanda y uno de los jóvenes más constantes del calendario africano, buscará en el Mundial de Canadá un escaparate para los equipos europeos de cara a 2027
articles.body: Canadá como punto de inflexión. El joven ciclista etíope Amaniel Desta acude a la cita con la selección de su país y con una incertidumbre a cuestas: el Team Amani, el equipo que le vio crecer y le abrió las puertas de la alta competición, no seguirá en 2027. Se apaga la casa que lo cobijó y toca buscar otra donde seguir pedaleando el sueño. Ese sueño tiene nombre de continente: Europa. Pero Desta no emprende la búsqueda con las manos vacías ni con la sola fuerza de la ilusión. Lleva en la maleta argumentos que se escriben en las carreteras. Su cuarto puesto en la general del Tour de Ruanda fue el gran resultado de su temporada y algo más: un punto de inflexión. Allí se midió con corredores de los mejores equipos de desarollo y salió con la cabeza alta, lo justo para que algunos ojos se posaran en él. A lo largo del año ha sostenido además una regularidad rara en un corredor tan joven, siempre cerca de los mejores, siempre entre los jóvenes que se dejan ver. Esa constancia pesa todavía más si se mira el camino recorrido para lograrla. “Mi experiencia en Team Amani ha sido muy buena para desarrollar mis habilidades y competir al más alto nivel”, explica a MARCA. Porque la ruta no ha sido llana. Ha habido caídas, fracturas y una escasez que se ha colado en lo más elemental: la comida, el techo, el transporte. “Ha habido momentos en los que no tenía suficiente dinero para la comida, el alquiler, el transporte o incluso para poder disponer de los medios necesarios durante los entrenamientos, llegando a situaciones de tener que entrenar con un simple plátano y azucarillos para poder completar el entrenamiento”, relata. Amaniel sabe que la línea de salida no es la misma para todos. Que hay jóvenes que arrancan con el viento a favor y otros que lo hacen de cara. “Hay una gran diferencia entre las oportunidades que tiene un joven ciclista africano y las que tiene un ciclista de mi edad en Europa. Los corredores europeos tienen mejores condiciones para entrenar, más apoyo y mucha más experiencia en competición. Nosotros no tenemos las mismas oportunidades”. Por eso la desaparición del Team Amani es un golpe duro. Pero un final también puede ser un comienzo. “Los corredores africanos no tenemos suficientes oportunidades para dar este salto y son muy limitadas. Pero aprovecharé la oportunidad si encuentro a alguien que quiera ayudarme”. Ahí entra el Mundial Sub-23 de Canadá, que para Desta será mucho más que una carrera: una ventana abierta al mundo, con equipos, directores deportivos y ojeadores mirando al otro lado del cristal. Quiere que esa mirada le encuentre en forma. Quiere demostrar, pedalada a pedalada, que lo de esta temporada no fue casualidad, que hay base y hay piernas para dar un paso más. Llegará a tierras canadienses tras meses de trabajo y de obstáculos que muchos de sus rivales ni imaginan, con un propósito sencillo: competir, disfrutar de vestir la camiseta de su país en un Mundial y llamar la atención de quien esté dispuesto a apostar por él en 2027. “Les pediría a los equipos que son reacios a contratar a un ciclista africano que nos den una oportunidad”. Porque un contrato en 2027 no sería solo un cambio de maillot. Sería la diferencia entre seguir y quedarse a un lado del camino. “Personalmente, conseguir un contrato en 2027 significa mucho para mí. Si no me ayudan ahora, puedo perder mi objetivo”. Amaniel Desta no pide que le regalen nada. Pide una oportunidad. La de entrenar en mejores condiciones, la de correr con regularidad en Europa, la de seguir creciendo. Y, sobre todo, la de demostrar que el talento no entiende de fronteras. Primero, Canadá. Después, si la fortuna y los equipos acompañan, Europa. Y Amaniel está dispuesto a pedalear hasta ella. Desta acaba de cumplir 21 años -nació el 19 de septiembre de 2005- y su realidad competitiva también ayuda a entender esa brecha. Team Amani, registrado en Ruanda y formado por corredores de distintos países africanos, no dispone del mismo calendario ni de la misma estructura que los grandes equipos de desarrollo europeos. Su programa se construye alrededor de un número más reducido de carreras internacionales y cada oportunidad tiene un valor enorme. El Tour de Ruanda fue el gran escaparate de su temporada: Desta terminó cuarto de la general, a 3:13 del vencedor, y además fue distinguido como mejor corredor africano y mejor joven africano. Para jóvenes como él, competir fuera de África supone además afrontar desplazamientos, costes y una logística que condicionan la cantidad y la calidad de las carreras que pueden disputar. Mientras muchos talentos europeos pasan la temporada encadenando pruebas con equipos de desarrollo, concentraciones y competiciones frente a estructuras WorldTour, el calendario africano ofrece menos ocasiones para mostrarse ante quienes toman las decisiones. El propio Team Amani nació con esa filosofía: crear una plataforma que permita a corredores de países como Etiopía, Ruanda, Uganda o Kenia competir a un nivel superior y acercarse al ciclismo profesional. El Mundial de Canadá representa, por tanto, una de esas pocas ventanas en las que Desta puede medirse en el mismo escenario y bajo la misma mirada que los mejores jóvenes del mundo.

articles.title: Alaba ficha por Udinese tras su salida del Real Madrid
articles.standfirst: Firma con el club italiano por una temporada. "He vivido muchas experiencias y he ganado mucho a lo largo de mi carrera, pero hay una cosa que no ha cambiado: quiero seguir ganando", dice
articles.summary: Firma con el club italiano por una temporada
articles.body: El defensa austríaco David Alaba fichó por el Udinese para una temporada como agente libre, después de poner fin a su etapa de cinco campañas en el Real Madrid, según informó este jueves el club italiano. "Jugador de extraordinaria calidad técnica, liderazgo y versatilidad táctica, Alaba llega a Udine después de una carrera desarrollada en la élite del fútbol mundial", informó la entidad del norte de Italia. El futbolista, de 34 años, llegó al conjunto madridista en 2021 procedente del Bayern Munich y disputó 132 partidos con el equipo blanco, en los que marcó cinco goles y conquistó once títulos. El defensa austríaco levantó con el Real Madrid dos Ligas de Campeones, dos Mundiales de Clubes, dos Supercopas de Europa, dos Ligas, una Copa del Rey y dos Supercopas de España. Su imagen con una silla en la cabeza durante la celebración de la victoria ante el Manchester City en las semifinales de la Liga de Campeones de 2022 se convirtió en una de las estampas más reconocibles de la llamada 'Champions de las remontadas'. De hecho, antes de oficializar el fichaje, la entidad italiana publicó en sus redes el miércoles una imagen de una silla plegable en mitad de un terreno de juego como guiño a este gesto. Alaba se formó en las categorías inferiores del Austria Viena, y a los 16 años fue fichado por el Bayern Munich, con quien conquistó dos 'Champions', dos Mundiales de Clubes, dos Supercopas de Europa y diez Bundesligas, entre otros. Internacional con Austria desde los 17 años y con más de un centenar de partidos con su selección, Alaba afronta ahora una nueva etapa en el fútbol italiano con el club 'friuliano'. "He vivido muchas experiencias y he ganado mucho a lo largo de mi carrera, pero hay una cosa que no ha cambiado: quiero seguir ganando. Quiero seguir compitiendo. Y quiero volver a conseguir algo especial. Esa es la mentalidad que llevo al Udinese", dijo el jugador, en declaraciones recogidas por el club.

articles.title: El Zaragoza se queda sin Ander Herrera indefinidamente
articles.standfirst: El capitán sufre una lumbalgia persistente
articles.summary: El capitán sufre una lumbalgia persistente
articles.body: Se esperaba que Ander Herrera causara baja este viernes por segunda jornada consecutiva por unos problemas en la espalda. Sin embargo, su ausencia se va a prolongar en el tiempo de manera indefinida después del parte médico que ha emitido el Real Zaragoza esta mañana. El capitán padece una lumbalgia persistente, tras las pruebas que se ha realizado. "Ander se someterá próximamente a tratamientos específicos para controlar su dolor y la evolución que presente marcará su disponibilidad para reincorporarse al grupo", indicó el comunicado del club aragonés. Por tanto, no hay fecha de regreso. Las lesiones vuelven a perseguir al zaragozano, que le han acompañado en las últimas temporadas. Ibai Gómez se ha referido a este tema en rueda de prensa: "Ander lo ha intentado esta semana. Le han mirado y no sabemos cuánto tiempo va a estar, pero espero que esté cuanto antes porque aporta mucho en todos los sentidos". Así que se espera que repitan en la medular tanto Ademo como Terrer y Rubén Díez. El técnico ha reconocido que empieza a sentir lo mismo que con el Arenas, con el que logró el ascenso: "Me recuerda a las sensaciones en el Arenas hace dos temporadas, de que todos van, todos quieren, se entienden mejor, son más precisos y son muy buenos. Tengo la sensación de que matarían por los compañeros. Ponen lo colectivo por encima de lo individual".

articles.title: Andy Carroll: Former England striker reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
articles.summary: Former England striker Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021, by a man who has subsequently been jailed for three years.
articles.body:
Former England striker Andy Carroll has revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021.

The 37-year-old, who was automatically granted anonymity as a victim of sexual assault, has made the details public in an autobiography titled 'Owning it'.

The incident took place at Carroll's home, during his second spell with his hometown club Newcastle and led to the perpetrator being jailed for three years.

Carroll, now a player/co-owner of non-league club Dagenham & Redbridge, says he decided to include the incident in his book "at the very last minute" after discussing it with his girlfriend Lou Teasdale.

A friend of his former partner, who was away at the time, was set to stay over after coming to his home to watch a boxing match.

Carroll says the incident occurred while he was sleeping and he then threw the man out of the house, before knocking him unconscious as he tried to return.

Carroll, who also played in the Premier League for Liverpool and West Ham, called the police and was "sobbing" in the arms of his children's nanny.

The unnamed attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offender register. Carroll testified in court, a process he says was "humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous".

Carroll wrote: "I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.

"Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

"Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."

Carroll, who won nine England caps, added: "What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I'd think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football… The trauma of what happened to me hasn't gone away."

Carroll joined Dagenham in July 2025 and has made six appearances in the National League South this season.

articles.title: Hibernian appoint Marink Reedijk: Thirty-five year old Dutchman arrives at Easter Road after success in Belgium
articles.summary: Marink Reedijk appointed as successor to David Gray after leading SK Beveren to an unbeaten title-winning season in Belgium's second tier; Hibs are 10th in Scottish Premiership with two wins from seven games
articles.body:
Dutchman Reedijk arrives from SK Beveren, having won the Belgian second-tier title with an unbeaten campaign.

The 35-year-old has also worked in academy positions at Ajax and West Bromwich Albion.

Reedijk, said: "I am honoured to be appointed manager of Hibernian Football Club.

"This is one of the biggest clubs in Scottish football, with a unique history, identity and supporter base, and I am excited to experience that passion and connection first-hand.

"I can feel the ambition and see the clarity of what the club is trying to achieve. That was a big part of what attracted me here.

"I want us to be an assertive team - brave, intense and committed. A team that gives everything, plays with purpose and gives our supporters something to really get behind.

"There is quality and potential in the squad, and good work has already been done. My first job is to get to know the players, build on those foundations and make sure we are ready for Dundee United."

Reedijk will now travel to La Manga with the team on Saturday for a training camp, with his first match a Scottish Premiership trip to Dundee United on October 10.

Hibs are currently 10th in the Scottish Premiership, with just two wins from their opening seven fixtures.

Hibernian sporting director, Malky Mackay , said: "Marink's appointment is an exciting moment for Hibernian Football Club.

"We began this process with a clear idea of the type of team we want to continue to build and the qualities we wanted from our next Manager. Marink's football philosophy, his work with players and his leadership style are strongly aligned with that.

"His teams are proactive, high energy and dynamic. What also stands out is his ability to develop individuals and create a strong collective environment.

"This is not about changing the direction of our football strategy. It is about continuing to evolve it, and we believe Marink is an excellent fit to take the team forward."

Hibernian executive chairman, Ian Gordon , said: "Marink was the standout candidate. He impressed everyone involved in the process with his clarity, intelligence and drive.

"He shares our ambition to develop players and consistently compete at the top end of Scottish football and in Europe.

"Marink has our backing, and we will continue to invest in the team to give him the best possible platform to succeed.

"We're delighted to welcome Marink and his family to the club."

articles.title: Xavi Espart: "Estar con la selección absoluta sería increíble, ahí están los mejores"
articles.standfirst: El canterano disfruta gran momento en el Barça y su citación con la sub 21
articles.summary: El canterano disfruta gran momento en el Barça y su citación con la sub 21
articles.body: Xavi Espart es una de las grandes revelaciones de la temporada. El joven defensa, concentrado con el combinado nacional sub 21, se ha ganado la confianza de Hansi Flick y es protagonista en el primer equipo azulgrana. El canterano culé habla, para la RFEF, de su inicio de curso con el Barça, de la selección... Sorpresa "Soy muy joven y poder jugar tantos minutos en el Barça no lo esperaba, pero sí sabía que, si llegaba el momento, era capaz". Entorno "Mis amigos y mi familia, siendo ellos muy del Barça, están flipando. Me hace sentir muy orgulloso ver que están tan felices por mis éxitos". Posición "Lo primero que soy es jugador. He jugado toda la vida como pivote, pero en cadete de segundo año me pusieron de lateral derecho y lo hice bien. Fui subiendo y lo hacía como lateral, pero si faltaba un medio me podían poner ahí. Eso gustó bastante y en el Barça he jugado de lateral izquierdo, puedo jugar de interior… Al principio me costaba bastante. Tenía asumido que jugaba de lateral y si me ponían de ‘6’ me costaba adaptarme. Pero te acostumbras. Siempre he dicho que lo importante es jugar". Sub 21 "Tenemos un equipazo, jugadores de una calidad excelente y fuera del campo nos llevamos muy bien". Absoluta "Estar ahí con la absoluta sería increíble, ahí están los mejores. Es algo que sueñas desde que eres pequeño". Sub19 “He disfrutado siempre de estar con la selección, es un orgullo y estoy muy contento".

articles.title: El Málaga decide esperar a enero para firmar un sustituto de Lobete
articles.standfirst: El club no ve claro el mercado de jugadores libres
articles.summary: El club no ve claro el mercado de jugadores libres
articles.body: El Málaga tiene decidido esperar a enero para cubrir la baja de Julen Lobete. Así lo ha podido saber Radio MARCA Málaga. El club blanquiazul no contempla, salvo un cambio de última hora, acudir al mercado de jugadores libres durante los próximos días. La dirección deportiva y el cuerpo técnico han analizado los numerosos ofrecimientos recibidos desde el cierre del mercado. Algunos nombres, como Zaha o Martial, llegaron a estar sobre la mesa, pero ninguno ha convencido al Málaga para realizar una apuesta inmediata. El club considera que el mercado de agentes libres ofrece ahora pocas garantías. Hay futbolistas sin ritmo competitivo y otros cuyas pretensiones económicas están muy por encima de los parámetros de Martiricos. En el caso de Martial, por ejemplo, sus exigencias salariales duplicaban las del jugador mejor pagado de la plantilla, según ha podido saber Radio MARCA Málaga. La postura de Funes también ha sido clara: no quiere que el club se precipite. "Tomar decisiones precipitadas puede llevar al error, pero necesitamos que el que venga tenga un rendimiento inmediato", señaló recientemente. El Málaga dispone de 20 días desde la operación de Lobete para solicitar la sustitución de su ficha ante LaLiga. Ese plazo se utilizará para estudiar el mercado, pero la hoja de ruta está marcada: esperar a enero y recuperar mientras tanto a los jugadores lesionados.

articles.title: Un 'respiro' para Kang-in Lee
articles.standfirst: Erigido en un fijo para Simeone tras un mes de competición, el surcoreano se 'libra' del primer compromiso de su selección después de un mes y medio de 'maratón' como rojiblanco
articles.summary: Erigido en un fijo para Simeone tras un mes de competición, el surcoreano se 'libra' del primer compromiso de su selección después de un mes y medio de 'maratón' como rojiblanco
articles.body: Después del vertiginoso mes y medio desde que se uniera al Atlético en Seúl hasta que finalizara el derbi erigido en uno de los mayores argumentos para que los rojiblancos luchen esta temporada por los títulos, Kang-in Lee por fin encuentra un momento para el respiro. No demasiado, pues en los próximos días le aguardan tres compromisos con su selección frente a Uruguay (el lunes 28), Venezuela (viernes 2 de octubre) y Uzbekistán (martes 6), pero al menos se ha librado del que Corea del Sur ha disputado este jueves frente a Ecuador. Consciente de la carga que lleva en las piernas después de ser uno de los nueve rojiblancos que ha participado en todos los partidos del Atlético (es el sexto más utilizado por Simeone tras emplearlo 528 minutos) y de que se trata de su mayor activo en su debut al frente del combinado asiático, Robert Moreno ha optado por conceder descanso a Kang in tras las más de 12 horas de vuelo desde Madrid que siguieron al triunfo del domingo. De hecho, tras incorporarse a la concentración más tarde que sus compañeros, tampoco participarían en el amistoso frente a Ecuador ni Hwang In-Beom (Oporto) ni Cho Gue-Sung (Midtjylland). Un 'alivio' también para un cuerpo técnico del Atlético que no ha tenido duda desde el primer día de la proyección que puede tener el surcoreano como rojiblanco. Así, pese a que apenas trabajaría dos semanas con el grupo antes del estreno liguero, Kang in ya irrumpiría en la segunda mitad para debutar con un golazo que suponía su mejor carta de presentación. Desde entonces, encadena siete titularidades, pese a que ha tenido que ir adquiriendo su mejor tono físico al mismo tiempo que competía (sólo podría disputar los 90 minutos ante Osasuna), en las que no ha hecho más que confirmar que no podía haber nadie mejor para enfundarse el 7 de Griezmann. De hecho, ya siendo segundo punta o extremo derecho, Kang in ya ha firmado dos goles, una asistencia y ha repartido 108 pases en la zona de ataque que dan fe de su influencia en el Atlético.
